title: Running local LLMs on a laptop
excerpt: Small quantized models now run offline on modest hardware. Here is what actually works.
author: Daniel Ortiz
caption: Cover photo via Picsum placeholder

body.x: A year ago, running a capable language model locally meant a workstation. Today, **4-bit quantized** models of 7 to 8 billion parameters run comfortably on 16 GB of RAM.
Pick the right format
GGUF files load in llama.cpp and its many frontends. Look for *Q4_K_M* quantization as a good balance between size and quality.

items: Start with a 7B model at Q4
Test on your actual machine before relying on it

body.x: A minimal load command

llama-cli -m model.Q4_K_M.gguf \
  -p "Explain vector search" \
  -n 256
Local models trade raw capability for privacy and zero latency.

title: Prompt engineering that survives production
excerpt: Prompts are code. Treat them with versioning, tests and clear contracts.
author: Maya Rahman
caption: Cover photo via Picsum placeholder

body.x: The demo prompt that impressed everyone in a meeting is rarely the prompt that survives real users. Production prompts need **structure**.
Define an output contract
Ask for JSON with a fixed schema, then validate it. Never trust a model to follow *implied* rules.

items: Keep a golden test set of inputs
Log inputs and outputs for review

body.x: Separate instructions from data
Wrap user content in clear delimiters so the model cannot confuse it with instructions. This also reduces prompt injection risk.
A prompt without tests is a guess with extra steps.

author: Daniel Ortiz

body.x: The `satisfies` operator checks a value against a type without changing the inferred type. It is the tool you want when annotations are too blunt.

title: RAG without a vector database
excerpt: For small corpora, keyword scoring and a simple index beat heavy infrastructure.
author: Priya Nair
caption: Cover photo via Picsum placeholder

body.x: Retrieval augmented generation does not require a managed vector store. If your corpus is under a few thousand documents, **BM25** plus a reranker works well.
Start simple

items: Add embeddings only when recall drops

body.x: The complexity budget is better spent on **evaluation** than on infrastructure. Measure whether retrieved chunks actually answer the question.
Retrieval quality is a data problem before it is an infrastructure problem.

title: What AI coding assistants are actually good at
excerpt: An honest look at where they help and where they quietly cost you time.
author: Maya Rahman
caption: Cover photo via Picsum placeholder

body.x: AI assistants excel at **boilerplate**, test scaffolding and explaining unfamiliar code. They struggle with architecture and long-lived state.
Where they save time
Where they cost time
Subtle bugs in generated code can take longer to debug than writing it yourself. Always review *security-sensitive* paths by hand.
Treat generated code like a pull request from a fast, confident stranger.

title: Edge functions: when they help and when they do not
excerpt: Latency wins are real, but so are the constraints on runtime and data access.
author: Priya Nair
caption: Cover photo via Picsum placeholder

body.x: Edge functions run close to users, cutting round-trip time. But they come with **cold starts**, limited APIs and awkward database access.
Good fits
Poor fits
Long-running jobs and heavy database transactions belong on a *regional* server. Measure before moving logic to the edge.

author: Daniel Ortiz

body.x: Web components now work well across frameworks. The question is whether the **encapsulation** is worth the ergonomics you give up.
Strengths
Trade-offs
